title: A microbe survives about 1,000 times the radiation that would kill you
body: Deinococcus radiodurans turned up in 1956, when Arthur Anderson in Oregon found a tin of meat had spoiled despite gamma rays meant to sterilise it. The microbe tolerates about 5,000 grays of ionising radiation with almost no loss of viability, while around 5 grays is enough to kill a person. Its secret isn’t avoiding damage but **repairing it**: each cell keeps several copies of its genome, so shattered fragments can be matched up and reassembled, and manganese complexes soak up the chemical damage. It also survives cold, dehydration, vacuum and acid.

slides.label: of ionising radiation, survived with almost no loss of viability
slides.text: About 5 Gy kills a human. Even at 12,000 Gy, roughly 10% of these bacteria, Deinococcus radiodurans, pull through.

slides.heading: Radiation doses, in grays
slides.note: About 5 Gy kills a person; D. radiodurans shrugs off 5,000 Gy with almost no loss of viability

slides.heading: How it survives
items: Four to ten copies of its genome per cell, so broken fragments can be pieced back together
Manganese complexes that act as antioxidants
Also survives cold, dehydration, vacuum and acid: a polyextremophile

events.text: Found in irradiated canned meat by Arthur Anderson in Oregon
Listed by Guinness World Records as the most radiation-resistant organism known

slides.question: Why can Deinococcus radiodurans take such a dose?
options: A thick shell blocks the rays
It repairs its DNA from spare copies
It has no DNA to damage
slides.explanation: The radiation shatters its DNA like anyone else’s. With four to ten genome copies per cell and manganese antioxidants, it rebuilds.
